raw_findings.message: Generated codes use predictable Math.random() output, so an attacker can guess unlisted links and code collisions are more likely than with a cryptographic generator.
Eight-character aliases pass validation but are silently truncated to seven characters, so the returned code differs from the alias the caller requested.
Expiry is stored in milliseconds but isExpired compares it with seconds, so links created with a TTL remain live long after they should expire.
Setting a code without checking whether it already exists silently replaces the prior link when an alias is reused or a generated code collides.
On the creation day, days is zero, so clicksPerDay becomes NaN and is serialized as null instead of a numeric statistic.
An unknown code makes the map lookup return undefined, which is cast to Link and dereferenced, causing the stats endpoint to return 500.
The admin token is a fixed source-code secret, so anyone who can read the project can authenticate to delete links.
When preview is enabled, the server fetches the user-supplied target without restricting destinations, allowing requests to loopback or other internal services.
Concurrent requests snapshot the same click count before awaiting file writes and then overwrite each other with the same increment, undercounting clicks.
TTL values are accepted without a representable-date range check, so a value such as 1e13 creates a link whose stats call throws when converting its expiry to ISO format.
Targets with schemes such as javascript: pass validation and are emitted as redirect locations, allowing a short link to trigger script execution in a browser.
Aliases are stored in lowercase but redirect lookups use the path code unchanged, so requesting a mixed-case alias that was accepted at creation returns 404.

fixed_raw_findings.message: `Number.isInteger` accepts very large finite values such as `1e308`, which can create an expiry outside JavaScript's valid `Date` range and make `/stats/:code` fail with a 500.
A link remains live when `now` equals `expiresAt`, so a link can still redirect at its stated expiry time instead of expiring when that time is reached.
The host is checked before `fetch`, which resolves it again, so an attacker-controlled DNS name can resolve publicly during validation and to a private address during the fetch when `preview: true`.
The preview reads the entire response body without a size limit, so concurrent preview requests to hosts serving large or endless responses can exhaust server memory.
Non-number `ttlSeconds` values are silently treated as omitted, so a request such as `{"ttlSeconds":"1"}` creates a permanent link instead of rejecting the invalid TTL.

raw_findings.message: Math.random() is not a cryptographically secure source, so generated codes can be predicted and used to access links and their statistics.
URL parsing accepts schemes such as javascript:, which can then be emitted as a redirect Location and potentially execute attacker-controlled script in a visitor's browser.
Eight-character aliases are accepted but truncated to seven characters, so the requested alias does not resolve and can collide with a different alias.
The map is updated without checking whether the code already exists, so creating a link with an existing alias silently replaces its target.
expiresAt is stored in milliseconds but compared with now in seconds, so links with a positive TTL do not expire when their expiry time passes.
Aliases are stored in lowercase but looked up using the request's original case, so a mixed-case request for a documented case-insensitive alias returns 404.
For links created less than one full day ago, days is zero and clicksPerDay becomes non-finite, which JSON serialization returns as null.
An unknown code makes the map lookup undefined, which is dereferenced and causes the stats endpoint to return a 500 instead of a not-found response.
The fixed admin token is embedded in source, allowing anyone who obtains the code to authenticate to the delete endpoint.
When preview is requested, the server fetches the user-supplied URL without restricting destinations, allowing requests to loopback, private-network, or other internal services.
Concurrent redirects can all read the same click count before awaiting the log write and then store the same incremented value, losing clicks.
A ttlSeconds value of zero is falsy and is stored as no expiry, so a link requested with a zero TTL remains live indefinitely.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The TTL check accepts very large integer values that overflow the valid JavaScript `Date` range when stats formats the expiry, causing `/stats/:code` to return 500 for that link.
A link is considered live when `now` equals `expiresAt`, so a request at the exact expiration second can still redirect instead of treating the link as expired.

The preview fetch resolves the hostname again after `assertPublicHost` checks its DNS answers, so a hostname that changes from a public address to a private one can make `preview: true` fetch an internal service.
Preview reads the entire response into memory even though it only returns a 200-character snippet, so an attacker-controlled target that streams a large body can exhaust server memory.
A supplied non-number `ttlSeconds` is silently treated as absent, so a request such as `{"ttlSeconds":"10"}` creates a link that never expires instead of rejecting the invalid TTL.
Deletion looks up the raw code without lowercasing it, so an admin cannot delete an existing mixed-case alias using a differently cased code despite aliases being case-insensitive elsewhere.

raw_findings.message: Generated link codes use predictable `Math.random()`, so an attacker can predict or enumerate codes and access links that rely on their secrecy.
Eight-character aliases are accepted but truncated to seven characters, so links created with such aliases cannot be reached using the alias the client supplied.
Expiry is stored in milliseconds while lookups compare it with seconds, so TTL links do not expire under normal use.
Creating a link unconditionally replaces any existing entry with the same code, allowing a user to hijack another user's alias by creating it again.
When a link is less than one full day old, `days` is zero and the click rate becomes `NaN` or `Infinity`, which is serialized as `null`.
The admin token is embedded in source, so anyone who can inspect the application can authenticate to the delete endpoint.
When preview is enabled, the server fetches the user-supplied URL without restricting destinations, allowing requests to localhost or other internal services and exposing response snippets.
Concurrent redirects read the same click count before awaiting the log write, so their subsequent increments overwrite one another and undercount clicks.
Targets are not restricted to HTTP(S), so a link can redirect users to a `javascript:` URL that may execute script in a browser.
The stats handler does not check whether the requested code exists, so requesting stats for an unknown code dereferences `undefined` and returns a 500 error.

Aliases are stored in lowercase but redirect lookups use the path code unchanged, so requesting an alias with different capitalization returns 404 despite aliases being documented as case-insensitive.

fixed_raw_findings.message: Anyone can repeatedly call the public shorten endpoint with distinct links, growing this in-memory map without a limit until the process runs out of memory.
A link is considered live when `now` exactly equals `expiresAt`, so a request during that second can use a link after its expiration time.
Very large integer TTLs are accepted but can produce an out-of-range JavaScript date here, causing stats requests for the created link to fail with a 500.
The hostname is checked before `fetch` resolves it again, so a rebinding DNS name can pass the public-address check and then make the preview request reach a private address.
An unauthenticated caller can request previews of public servers that stream arbitrarily large bodies, and `res.text()` buffers the entire response into memory.
Anyone can repeatedly request a live redirect to append indefinitely to the click log, potentially exhausting the server's disk.
A supplied non-number `ttlSeconds` is silently treated as omitted, allowing malformed requests such as `{"ttlSeconds":"60"}` to create links that never expire.
Aliases are documented and looked up case-insensitively, but deleting an alias with different capitalization fails because this lookup is case-sensitive.
